summary: Discusses two TCP extensions for networks with a high bandwidth times delay product: a larger window and a negative acknowledgment. They were implemented and tested at NASA. It is experimental, and now historic. It was replaced by RFC 6247.

plainLanguage.summary: On a very long, fast pipe, you can send lots before hearing back. This asks for bigger batches and a way to say "that piece was missing."

questions: how does tcp perform on satellite links
what is the bandwidth delay product
tcp extensions for high delay networks
subtitle: Negative acknowledgments and 32-bit windows for high-bandwidth networks.

tldr.problem: On satellite and other high-delay networks, a single lost packet causes catastrophic throughput loss because TCP must time out and retransmit everything, and a 16-bit window (64 kilobytes) is too small to fill the pipe.
tldr.mechanism: Two TCP extensions—negative acknowledgment (NAK) to signal lost data and a big window option to expand the window to 32 bits (over 1 gigabyte)—improve recovery and allow larger data in flight.
tldr.outcome: These extensions were tested at NASA on T1 satellite channels. Performance improved significantly in the presence of errors when NAK and big windows are used together, though they remain experimental and have been superseded by RFC 6247.

today: RFC 1106 is Historic and experimental. While the specific NAK and big window options are no longer used, the broader ideas—larger windows and explicit loss signaling—have been incorporated into more general solutions. RFC 6247 consolidated the lessons from RFC 1072 and 1106 into a unified, modern approach for high-bandwidth networks.

sections.title: The Problem on High-Delay Networks
sections.content:
RFC 1106 tackles the same high bandwidth-delay product problem as RFC 1072, but proposes different solutions based on experience at NASA. The author notes that on satellite networks with 600 millisecond round-trip delay or transcontinental DS3 lines, the bandwidth-delay product exceeds 10 to the 6th power bits, beyond TCP's original design.

The core issue is that when a packet is lost, TCP cannot tell the sender which other packets survived. The sender must wait for a timeout or use duplicate ACKs to guess that a loss occurred. On a satellite with multi-second delays, by the time the sender learns of the loss and retransmits, the window has emptied. The sender then refills the pipe, wasting at least three times the one-way delay in bandwidth.
sections.plainLanguage: When a satellite loses one packet, standard TCP waits forever (a few seconds) before noticing. By then, the window is empty and the sender has to wait and refill it, wasting time.

sections.title: Why NAK Instead of SACK?
sections.content:
RFC 1106 compares two approaches to inform the sender about lost packets: selective acknowledgments (SACK) and negative acknowledgments (NAK).

SACK tells the sender which pieces arrived safely. NAK tells the sender which piece is missing. NAK is simpler: the receiver tracks only the first missing segment, not a list of received blocks. The option says "I need this segment number" and a count of how many following segments are missing. This requires less state and less CPU to generate.

However, SACK has one advantage: when multiple packets are lost close together, the sender learns about all of them at once. With NAK, the sender learns about losses one at a time, requiring extra processing. The author argues that in practice, packet losses are far enough apart that this advantage is rarely seen, and the simplicity of NAK makes it the better choice for satellite environments.

Note: RFC 1072 had already proposed SACK; this RFC proposes NAK as an alternative.
sections.plainLanguage: NAK is like the receiver saying "please send segment number 5," while SACK says "I got segments 1-4 and 6-10." NAK is easier to implement and works well when losses are rare and spread out.

sections.title: The NAK Option
sections.content:
The NAK option consists of a sequence number of the first byte not received and a count of segments needing to be resent. When the receiver detects a gap in sequence numbers, it sends a NAK option. Since NAK is advisory and unreliable, the sender may choose to ignore it and rely on timeout instead; if the NAK itself is lost, the retransmission timer will eventually fire.

The receiver tracks the last NAK sent to avoid repeating it: if every segment arrival triggered the same NAK, the sender would needlessly retransmit the same data over and over. However, by the time the NAK is received and processed, the pipe may be large enough that many additional NAKs could be in flight for the same missing segment.

The RFC notes that empirical testing shows the likelihood of a NAK being lost is small, so this simple advisory approach works well in practice.
sections.plainLanguage: When a gap appears in the received data, the receiver sends a NAK saying "I need starting from byte 5000." The sender resends that data immediately instead of waiting for a timeout.

sections.title: Big Window Option
sections.content:
The big window option expands the window from 16 bits (64 kilobytes maximum) to 30 bits (over 1 gigabyte). The mechanism is simple: the option carries the upper 15 bits of the receive window, while the lower 16 bits go in the standard TCP header field.

Both sides must agree to use big windows by exchanging the option in their SYN segments. Once negotiated, every packet thereafter includes the big window option containing the current upper bits.

The RFC notes this approach is more elegant than alternatives like window multipliers or streaming, because it is a true extension of the window mechanism that could eventually become part of the protocol itself, not just an option.
sections.plainLanguage: The standard TCP window is 16 bits. The option adds 15 more bits, making 31 total, so the window can grow to gigabytes instead of kilobytes.

sections.title: Using NAK and Big Windows Together
sections.content:
The RFC includes test results from NASA showing the performance gains when both options are used. On a 1.544 Mbps satellite link with 580 milliseconds round-trip delay, the transfer rate without errors using big windows alone reached 160 kilobytes per second. With big windows and NAK, the rate remained similar but performance in the presence of errors improved dramatically.

At a 10-to-the-negative-7 error rate (one bit error per 10 million bits), big windows alone gave 45 kilobytes per second. With NAK and big windows, it jumped to 160 kilobytes per second, nearly matching the no-error case.

The RFC discusses a critical issue: the difference between congestion (too much traffic) and noise (line errors). NAK assumes losses are noise, not congestion. If the sender wrongly assumes a congestion loss is noise and keeps sending at full window, the network can collapse. The RFC recommends that applications using big windows on links with known low error rates use the slow-start congestion control mechanism to back off on any loss, treating it as potential congestion. On high-error satellite links, operators may need to configure TCP to treat noise-caused losses differently from congestion-caused losses.
sections.plainLanguage: When a satellite connection uses both NAK and big windows, it keeps data flowing even with errors. Without NAK, one lost packet caused the window to empty. With NAK, the sender resends just the missing packet and keeps sending new data.

sections.title: Implementation and Deployment
sections.content:
The RFC notes that implementing big windows requires changing 16-bit window variables in the TCP control block to 32-bit quantities. This is straightforward but requires care: expanding the structure could exceed the memory buffer used to hold it on some systems (such as 4.3 BSD).

Both options were implemented and tested at NASA. The document notes that systems implementing the options can communicate with systems that do not: non-understanding TCPs simply ignore the options and use default 16-bit windows, allowing backward compatibility.

A concern when using big windows is the consumption of memory buffers. When 2 times the bandwidth-delay product of data is unacknowledged on both ends, both systems must buffer it, a potentially scarce resource. NASA was implementing a way to allow applications to request big windows via setsockopt, restricting large windows to applications that truly need them.
sections.plainLanguage: The changes are not too hard to add to existing TCP code. Old systems still work with new systems; the new system just uses small windows when talking to an old one. But buffering a lot of data can use up machine memory, so big windows should be used carefully.
